\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models spanning three architecture families across three reasoning domains (FOLIO, ProofWriter, LogiQA), and over 2,400 evaluation instances with three-seed replication on the primary condition. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.21$--$0.82$ among instruction-tuned models (0.91 for thinking mode), and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. We observe a narrow favorable region around 50--55\% SC accuracy in one model-dataset condition (Mistral-7B on FOLIO): Mistral-7B on FOLIO shows a positive directional trend of $+3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.092$, 2 of 3 seeds marginal at $p < 0.10$, none reaching $p < 0.05$; 3-seed mean $+2.12$\,pp). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ is the only setting with $\Delta > 2$\,pp among five $K$ values, and only 1 of 4 temperature settings ($T = 0.7$) produces a positive effect; both peaks coincide with a relatively low SC baseline.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is limited to same-model self-extraction. We do not test trained FOL extractors, external solvers with verified grounding, or multi-model constraint pipelines, all of which may overcome the independence bottleneck. The observed favorable region is narrow (SC $\approx$ 50--55\%), observed in only one model-dataset condition, limiting practical applicability. The optimal $K$ and temperature settings cannot be determined without labeled data, as both sensitivity analyses show the best configuration coincides with the lowest SC baseline rather than following a predictable trend. Our evaluation covers formal reasoning benchmarks (FOLIO, ProofWriter, LogiQA) but lacks open-domain validation where formalizability is lower and failure modes may differ. Finally, three-seed replication applies only to the primary condition (Mistral-7B on FOLIO), where one of three seeds yields a null result, indicating that even the strongest positive finding is sensitive to sampling variance.

1	Several limitations bound the scope of our conclusions. First, the oracle experiments cover two formal logic benchmarks (FOLIO $n = 204$, ProofWriter $n = 600$) that provide gold annotations; extending this analysis to commonsense or science domains requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets for those domains. Second, seven of our eleven model-domain conditions have $n \leq 60$, providing insufficient statistical power for confirmatory claims; power analysis shows that the minimum detectable effect exceeds 5\,pp for these conditions (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:power}), so they serve as regime characterization rather than definitive tests. Third, we do not compare against trained FOL extractors or cross-model extraction pipelines; our findings characterize the limitations of same-model self-extraction specifically. Fourth, all models tested range from 7B to 32B parameters; whether the capability trap persists at larger scales (70B+) remains an open question. Fifth, our extraction prompts use a single zero-shot template per domain; alternative prompting strategies (few-shot exemplars, chain-of-thought extraction, or iterative refinement) might yield higher-quality constraints, though the oracle gap suggests the bottleneck is fundamental rather than prompt-specific. Sixth, the constraint quality analysis (91.8\% Z3 semantic discriminative rate, 8.2\% non-discriminative rate, 39.2\% source-trace minority weight) covers Qwen2.5-14B on the full FOLIO + ProofWriter dataset ($N = 804$); other model-domain combinations may exhibit different constraint characteristics. Seventh, constraint extraction uses $T_{\text{ext}} = 0.3$ while trace sampling uses $T = 0.7$; alternative extraction temperatures might yield different constraint characteristics, though our negative results suggest the bottleneck is semantic coupling rather than extraction diversity. Eighth, StrategyQA and ARC-Challenge use the mathematical extraction prompt rather than the logical one because their reasoning structure does not involve formal predicates or implications (Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}); a domain-specific commonsense extraction template might yield different constraint characteristics for these benchmarks. Ninth, although we prompt for FOL-style formalizations, the extracted constraints are predominantly propositional ground clauses without quantifiers (\S\ref{sec:constraint-extraction}); whether models capable of producing genuine quantified FOL would yield higher discriminative rates is untested. Tenth, deduplication uses syntactic equivalence, so semantically equivalent constraints with different surface forms receive separate weights, potentially inflating the apparent constraint pool without adding discriminative content. Eleventh, the GSM8K pilot ($n = 30$) is included to illustrate the constraint-absent failure regime and should not be interpreted as confirmatory evidence.

file.content: Several limitations bound the scope of our conclusions. First, the oracle experiments cover two formal logic benchmarks (FOLIO $n = 204$, ProofWriter $n = 600$) that provide gold annotations; extending this analysis to commonsense or science domains requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets for those domains. Second, seven of our eleven model-domain conditions have $n \leq 60$, providing insufficient statistical power for confirmatory claims; power analysis shows that the minimum detectable effect exceeds 5\,pp for these conditions (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:power}), so they serve as regime characterization rather than definitive tests. Third, we do not compare against trained FOL extractors or cross-model extraction pipelines; our findings characterize the limitations of same-model self-extraction specifically. Fourth, all models tested range from 7B to 32B parameters; whether the capability trap persists at larger scales (70B+) remains an open question. Fifth, our extraction prompts use a single zero-shot template per domain; alternative prompting strategies (few-shot exemplars, chain-of-thought extraction, or iterative refinement) might yield higher-quality constraints, though the oracle gap suggests the bottleneck is fundamental rather than prompt-specific. Sixth, the constraint quality analysis (91.8\% Z3 semantic discriminative rate, 8.2\% non-discriminative rate, 39.2\% source-trace minority weight) covers Qwen2.5-14B on the full FOLIO + ProofWriter dataset ($N = 804$); other model-domain combinations may exhibit different constraint characteristics. Seventh, constraint extraction uses $T_{\text{ext}} = 0.3$ while trace sampling uses $T = 0.7$; alternative extraction temperatures might yield different constraint characteristics, though our negative results suggest the bottleneck is semantic coupling rather than extraction diversity. Eighth, StrategyQA and ARC-Challenge use the mathematical extraction prompt rather than the logical one because their reasoning structure does not involve formal predicates or implications (Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}); a domain-specific commonsense extraction template might yield different constraint characteristics for these benchmarks. Ninth, although we prompt for FOL-style formalizations, the extracted constraints are predominantly propositional ground clauses without quantifiers (\S\ref{sec:constraint-extraction}); whether models capable of producing genuine quantified FOL would yield higher discriminative rates is untested. Tenth, deduplication uses syntactic equivalence, so semantically equivalent constraints with different surface forms receive separate weights, potentially inflating the apparent constraint pool without adding discriminative content. Eleventh, the GSM8K pilot ($n = 30$) is included to illustrate the constraint-absent failure regime and should not be interpreted as confirmatory evidence.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across six models spanning three architecture families across three reasoning domains (FOLIO, ProofWriter, LogiQA), and over 2,400 evaluation instances with three-seed replication on the primary condition. Grounded in the Condorcet Jury Theorem, our analysis explains why Self-Consistency majority voting saturates and why symbolic constraint aggregation fails to break this plateau under same-model self-extraction.

The central finding is the independence bottleneck. Same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa$ values of $0.21$--$0.82$ among instruction-tuned models (0.91 for thinking mode), and the effective sample size compresses to Eff-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ at $K = 12$. Self-extracted FOL constraints inherit this correlation structure. We observe a narrow favorable region around 50--55\% SC accuracy in one model-dataset condition (Mistral-7B on FOLIO): Mistral-7B on FOLIO shows a positive directional trend of $+3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.092$, 2 of 3 seeds marginal at $p < 0.10$, none reaching $p < 0.05$; 3-seed mean $+2.12$\,pp). Outside this zone, confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative (Type~A) or error amplification actively degrades accuracy by $-2.83$\,pp (Type~C).

Oracle controls confirm that the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The uniform failure confirms the bottleneck is structural rather than an engineering artifact. Sensitivity analysis reinforces this conclusion: $K = 12$ is the only setting with $\Delta > 2$\,pp among five $K$ values, and only 1 of 4 temperature settings ($T = 0.7$) produces a positive effect; both peaks coincide with a relatively low SC baseline.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost deployment diagnostic for predicting when symbolic aggregation can help. Three paths forward trade simplicity for independence as CJT requires: trained extractors, external provers, and multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is limited to same-model self-extraction. We do not test trained FOL extractors, external solvers with verified grounding, or multi-model constraint pipelines, all of which may overcome the independence bottleneck. The observed favorable region is narrow (SC $\approx$ 50--55\%), observed in only one model-dataset condition, limiting practical applicability. The optimal $K$ and temperature settings cannot be determined without labeled data, as both sensitivity analyses show the best configuration coincides with the lowest SC baseline rather than following a predictable trend. Our evaluation covers formal reasoning benchmarks (FOLIO, ProofWriter, LogiQA) but lacks open-domain validation where formalizability is lower and failure modes may differ. Finally, three-seed replication applies only to the primary condition (Mistral-7B on FOLIO), where one of three seeds yields a null result, indicating that even the strongest positive finding is sensitive to sampling variance.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective across tasks without additional training.
It is also hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models, a pattern consistent across model families and reasoning tasks.
The plateau is consequential: test-time compute is the primary knob available to practitioners who cannot retrain or scale model parameters, and if additional samples stop helping, aggregation-based scaling faces a hard limit.
The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch between the independence assumption underlying majority voting and the correlated nature of same-model traces.

Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions of SC alleviate this to a degree, but the core limitation persists.
Traces sampled from the same model carry correlated errors.
When most traces converge on the same (possibly wrong) answer, additional samples provide no new information, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct the shared bias.
Trained reward models \citep{lightman2024prm, wang2024mathshepherd} and diversity-aware sampling \citep{diverseaware2026} break this plateau by injecting external signal or controlling trace diversity, but require either trained verifiers or modifications to the sampling procedure.
A more fundamental question remains: can \emph{structured aggregation} over symbolic representations extract information from the same traces that majority voting cannot?
If symbolic representations capture logical relationships that natural language answers discard, aggregation over constraints could in principle recover signal that vote counting misses.

Recent neuro-symbolic methods suggest that formal reasoning can complement LLM generation.
Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \citep{olausson2023linc} translate natural language problems into first-order logic (FOL) for external provers.
More recent systems route problems to specialized solver paradigms \citep{xu2026dylos}, apply logic-complete decomposition \citep{li2025aristotle}, train dedicated FOL verifiers \citep{wang2025fover}, or employ multi-perspective grounding \citep{luo2025logicagent}.
These methods report gains on logical reasoning benchmarks, but each introduces components beyond the reasoning model itself: trained verifiers, multi-paradigm solver selection, or external knowledge bases.
A simpler question precedes these architectural extensions: can the \emph{same} model that generates reasoning traces also extract useful formal constraints from them?
If so, self-extraction would be a zero-cost upgrade to SC that requires no additional model, no training data, and no external prover.
Any LLM could be augmented with symbolic verification through a single extraction prompt and a satisfiability solver.
The appeal is practical: self-extraction scales with the base model, requires no domain-specific engineering, and preserves the simplicity that makes SC attractive in the first place.
Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extracted constraints are useful for aggregation, or characterized the conditions under which they succeed or fail.
This question motivates our study of Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}, which provides a formal lens for understanding when aggregation succeeds.
CJT states that if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority is correct with probability approaching 1 as $K$ grows \citep{austensmith1996}.
SC implicitly depends on this guarantee: when independence holds, more traces monotonically improve accuracy.
When it fails, as \citet{ladha1992correlated} show for correlated voters, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Same-model traces violate independence.
We measure inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa} and find values from 0.21 to 0.82 across instruction-tuned conditions (0.91 for thinking mode), yielding an effective sample size (Eff-$K$) of 1.20 to 3.62 for nominal $K = 12$ (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
In practical terms, 12 sampled traces from the same model carry the information of fewer than 4 independent opinions, and in the most correlated conditions, barely more than 1.
At Eff-$K \approx 1$, each additional trace is informationally redundant, and no aggregation method operating on those traces alone can escape the plateau.
Symbolic verification could in principle inject independent signal, because formal logic validity does not depend on the generative model.
But when the same model both produces the reasoning trace and extracts the formal constraint, the constraint inherits the trace's biases and errors \citep{huang2024selfcorrect, kambhampati2024position}.
Self-extracted constraints do not constitute an independent check; they are a reformulation of the same evidence.
We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}: the traces that produce constraints also determine their quality, so the constraints cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass SC.
Recent work has examined CJT violations in LLM ensembles \citep{lefort2024condorcet_llm}, but no prior study connects this theoretical framework to symbolic constraint extraction.
The distinction matters: symbolic constraints appear to introduce a qualitatively different information source (formal logic rather than natural language votes), yet our analysis shows that the extraction step collapses this apparent independence back into the shared model distribution.

We evaluate SICA across six models (7B to 32B parameters), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and more than 2,400 evaluation instances with three-seed replication on the primary condition (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
Our evaluation spans instruction-tuned and reasoning-specialized model variants to ensure the findings are not artifacts of a single model family.
The central finding is the independence bottleneck itself; as a secondary observation, we find positive directional trends in a narrow region around 50--55\% SC accuracy in one model-dataset condition (Mistral-7B on FOLIO, 2 of 3 seeds with $p < 0.10$, none reaching $p < 0.05$; best $+3.43$\,pp).
Outside it, three distinct failure modes emerge (\S\ref{sec:failure-modes}).
In Type~A conditions (SC $\geq$ 60\%), constraints exhibit confirmation bias and merely echo the majority answer; SICA provides no significant positive effect across eight conditions ($N > 2{,}200$ combined), and one condition shows significant degradation ($-2.50$\,pp, $p = 0.011$).
In Type~C conditions (SC $\leq$ 40\%), predominantly incorrect traces produce noisy constraints that actively degrade accuracy ($-2.83$\,pp, $p = 0.014$).
In Type~B conditions, domains that resist formalization yield no useful signal regardless of model accuracy.

Oracle controls causally localize the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
Replacing self-extracted constraints with gold FOL annotations produces $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound when constraints are discriminative.
Self-extraction captures only 24\% of this oracle ceiling; the gap localizes to extraction quality, not solver limitations.
We test nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions (prompting, architecture, capability, verification, diversity, and filtering), and all fail to widen the effective region (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
The bottleneck is structural: it cannot be resolved within the same-model self-extraction paradigm.
Sensitivity analysis provides further diagnostic evidence: SICA gain peaks at $K = 12$ (the only setting with $\Delta > 2$\,pp among five $K$ values) and at $T = 0.7$ (the only positive result among four temperatures). In both cases, the peak coincides with a relatively low SC baseline, suggesting that the underlying driver is the SC-level regime, not the hyperparameter itself (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
These patterns confirm that SICA's benefit is fragile, dependent on a precise balance of trace diversity and extraction quality that same-model sampling rarely achieves.
This paper presents a systematic empirical analysis of symbolic constraint aggregation, not a new method. Our goal is to characterize when and why self-extracted constraints fail, providing diagnostic tools and identifying the structural conditions under which future approaches must operate.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Independence Bottleneck.} We formalize the SC plateau through the Condorcet Jury Theorem: same-model traces yield Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ (Eff-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ for $K = 12$), quantifying why additional traces provide diminishing returns. Trace correlation affects symbolic aggregation through two channels: it directly limits voting diversity (explaining the SC plateau) and indirectly produces homogeneous constraints that cause MAX-SAT to degenerate to vote counting (explaining SICA's failure to surpass SC). Oracle controls disambiguate these channels (\S\ref{sec:condorcet}, \S\ref{sec:effective-k}).

\item \textbf{Oracle-Extraction Gap.} Oracle constraints yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound. Self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling. The failure localizes to extraction quality, not the symbolic approach (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
